subject: Physics
description: Ohm's law, series vs parallel, Kirchhoff's laws, power, fuses

questions.stem: Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor (at constant temperature) is:

options.option_text: Directly proportional to potential difference (V) across the conductor: V = I·R

questions.explanation: Ohm's Law (Georg Ohm, 1827): V = I·R. Constant of proportionality R = resistance (in ohms, Ω). Holds only for 'ohmic' materials at constant temperature; non-ohmic devices include diodes, transistors, gas-discharge tubes, filament bulbs at high T. Power dissipated P = V·I = I²·R = V²/R (joules per second = watts).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: When two resistors of resistance 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in PARALLEL, the equivalent resistance is:
questions.explanation: Parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 → R_eq = 2 Ω. Always smaller than the smallest individual resistance. Series: R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + … = 6 + 3 = 9 Ω (always larger than the largest individual). For two parallel resistors: shortcut R_eq = R₁·R₂/(R₁+R₂) = 6·3/9 = 2.

questions.stem: Domestic electrical appliances in India are connected in PARALLEL across the supply because:

options.option_text: Each device gets the same voltage; one device failing doesn't break the others; each can be switched independently

questions.explanation: Houses run on parallel circuits. Each appliance — bulb, fan, AC, fridge — sees the supply voltage 230 V. Currents add up in the main wire. If a bulb fuses, others still work. Independent on/off via individual switches. In a SERIES circuit, all elements share current; voltage divides; if any single bulb fuses, entire series goes off (older Christmas-tree lights work this way).

questions.stem: An electric fuse works on the principle of:

options.option_text: Heating effect of current — wire melts if current exceeds rating

questions.explanation: Fuse — short piece of wire (tin-lead alloy, low melting point ~200 °C) inserted in series with appliances. If current exceeds the rated value (e.g. 5A, 15A), I²·R heating melts the fuse, breaks the circuit — preventing fire/electrocution. Modern alternative: MCB (Miniature Circuit Breaker) — uses a bimetallic strip + electromagnetic trip, can be reset (vs fuse which must be replaced). RCCB / ELCB detects current LEAKAGE to ground (different mechanism).

questions.stem: An electric heater rated 1500 W operates on a 230 V supply. The current drawn is approximately:
questions.explanation: Power formula: P = V·I → I = P/V = 1500 / 230 ≈ 6.52 A. Resistance of heater = V/I = 230/6.52 ≈ 35.3 Ω. Power consumption per hour = 1.5 kWh = 1.5 'units' on the electricity bill. Rule of thumb — every kW of appliance load draws ~4.35 A on Indian 230 V supply.

questions.stem: Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) states that at any junction in an electric circuit:

options.option_text: Algebraic sum of currents = 0 (currents in = currents out)
Voltage drops add up to EMF

questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's two laws: (1) KCL (current law / junction rule): ∑I = 0 at any node — conservation of charge. (2) KVL (voltage law / loop rule): ∑V = 0 around any closed loop — conservation of energy. KCL implies whatever flows in must flow out. KVL implies the total potential gain (EMF) around a loop equals total potential drop (across resistors). Together they enable analysis of any DC circuit, however complex.

questions.stem: If the same current flows through two resistors connected in series, the larger resistor:

options.option_text: Dissipates more power (P = I²R, so larger R → more heat)

questions.explanation: Series: same current I through every element. Power dissipated by each resistor = I²R, so the LARGER resistance dissipates more power → gets hotter. In parallel: voltage is the same across both, current divides; P = V²/R, so the SMALLER resistor dissipates more power. This is the underpinning of why nichrome (high R) is used in heaters but copper (low R) in connecting wires.
